case.case_title: Sirimawathie Fernando v. Wickremaratne, Officer in Charge, Police Station, Dehiwela and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, SC Application No. 255/98, decided on 7 December 1999

clause.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Article 11 were violated by the police and municipal authorities through forcible eviction, arrest, and degrading treatment despite a court stay order.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed she was unlawfully evicted, arrested, assaulted, and subjected to degrading treatment by police officers and municipal employees, in defiance of a Court of Appeal stay order protecting her possession of the shop.
case_context.respondent_argument: The police respondents denied knowledge of the stay order at the time of arrest and claimed the petitioner obstructed official duties; the municipal respondents claimed they requested temporary vacation of premises and denied knowledge of the stay order.
key_facts: Petitioner’s sister was lawful lessee of shop No. 2 since 1967.
A Court of Appeal ex parte stay order was issued on 17.3.98 restraining eviction.
On 18.3.98, municipal employees and police officers attempted forcible eviction and fixed barbed wire at shop entrances.
Petitioner produced certified copy of stay order which was ignored and crumpled by police officer.
Petitioner was arrested, assaulted, taken to police station, and subjected to degrading treatment.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court held that Article 11 protects individuals from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, which includes unlawful arrest and assault by state agents. The police and municipal officers’ actions in ignoring a valid court order and subjecting the petitioner to assault and degrading treatment violated this constitutional protection.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found the police acted without verifying the legality of the eviction order, ignored the stay order, and arrested the petitioner unlawfully. The petitioner’s evidence of assault and degrading treatment was accepted over the police denials. The municipal mayor was held liable for instigating the illegal eviction without legal authority.
principles_established: State agents must respect court orders and fundamental rights when executing duties.
Unlawful arrest and assault by police constitute violations of Article 11.
Municipal authorities cannot bypass legal remedies and use police to effect illegal evictions.
Failure to verify legality of orders before enforcement breaches fundamental rights.

outcome.holding: The court held that the petitioner’s fundamental rights under Article 11 were violated by the 1st and 5th respondents and awarded compensation of Rs. 60,000, to be paid personally by the 1st and 5th respondents.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The 1st respondent (police officer) and the 5th respondent (Mayor) were each ordered to pay Rs. 30,000 as compensation before 30 April 2000.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 11 was central to the court’s reasoning as it directly protects against cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment, which the petitioner suffered through unlawful arrest, assault, and degrading treatment by police officers during the eviction.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was arrested despite producing a certified copy of a stay order, assaulted in the police jeep, and subjected to degrading treatment, all in the presence and with the acquiescence of the 1st respondent police officer.
